title: The three levels: how a 91-yard run happens (and why a loaded box is a gamble)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: "not configured for this session"). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson builds on Lesson 19 (count the box) and Lesson 20 (read the safeties), using Tuesday night's 91-yard touchdown run and Thursday's game, where Jacksonville will likely crowd the line against a rookie QB.

The big idea: a run defense has three layers, called levels.Level 1 is the defensive line. Level 2 is the linebackers. Level 3 is the safeties.A short run is stopped at level 1 or 2. A long touchdown run happens when the offense blocks the first two levels and the runner beats the last one.

Seen from behind the offense. White squares are the offensive line (LT, LG, C, RG, RT); white circles are the TE, QB and RB. Yellow circles are the defense: DL (defensive line), LB (linebackers), S (safeties). A, B and C match the steps below.

  1. Level 1: the line. The offensive line blocks the defensive line at the snap.Often two linemen block one defender together (a double-team). Then one of them lets go and moves up the field. Coaches call that climbing to the second level.A: the center and right tackle climb to block two linebackers.
  2. Level 2: the linebackers, 3 to 5 yards off the ball. Most runs are decided here.If the climbing blockers reach the linebackers, a hole opens past the line (Lesson 14 on gaps).B: the running back goes through that hole. Now he is 6 or 7 yards downfield with only the safeties left.
  3. Level 3: the safeties, 10 to 15 yards deep. They are the last line.When the defense puts 8 players in the box (Lesson 19), one safety has moved down near the line. That leaves only one deep safety.C: if that one safety misses, nobody is left. That is how a 10-yard run becomes a 91-yard touchdown.
  4. Tuesday night: Ohio at Akron. Akron led 17-14 with 9:35 left.Ohio answered with Nick Poulos's 60-yard TD pass to Dom Dorwart. Then Duncan Brune ran 91 yards for a TD with 3:57 left: 28-17 (ESPN).Both were third-level plays: the deep pass beat the safeties in the air, the run beat them on the ground. Final: Ohio 28, Akron 20.
  5. More real examples. Week 8 in the rain: Tampa Bay ran for a team-record 322 yards against Atlanta. Bucky Irving had 27 carries for 170.Week 7: Dallas's Javonte Williams ran for 155, the Cowboys' first 150-yard game since 2018. Runs like these come from blocks at level 2, not just at the line.
  6. The gamble, Thursday. Jacksonville faces Baltimore's undrafted rookie QB, Joe Fagnano, on a sore ankle.Expect the Jaguars to bring a safety down and play 8 in the box: they'd rather make a rookie throw.That makes Baltimore's runs short most of the time. But if a run gets past the linebackers, there's just one safety to beat. And a play-action deep shot (Lesson 16) has more room.

How to use it in your drill: before the snap, count the box (Lesson 19), then count the deep safeties (Lesson 20). 8 in the box with 1 deep safety means the defense expects a run. Log your run/pass call. After the play, ask: at which level was it stopped? Line, linebackers, or safeties? A play that reaches level 3 against one deep safety is the one that turns into a long gain.

Why it matters for your bets: long runs break totals and "longest rush" props. Ohio-Akron was a low-scoring game until two third-level plays in the last 10 minutes. It still stayed under 50.5, at 48. When you bet an Under against a team with a weak passer, remember the defense is crowding the line. That shortens most runs, but it leaves one man deep.

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): Thursday, Jaguars at Ravens (5:15 p.m., Prime Video): count Jacksonville's box against Fagnano. Saturday, Penn State at Washington (12:30 p.m., FS1): Penn State ran for 269 yards against Purdue; watch whether Washington drops a safety into the box.

Video: search YouTube for "three levels of defense explained," "offensive line climbing to the second level," and "Duncan Brune 91 yard touchdown Ohio Akron."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 2: The box)

quiz.q: What is the "second level" of a run defense?
o: The linebackers, 3 to 5 yards off the ball
quiz.w: Level 1 is the line, level 2 the linebackers, level 3 the safeties. Most runs are decided at level 2.

quiz.q: A defense puts 8 players in the box. How many deep safeties are usually left?
quiz.w: 11 players, minus 8 in the box, minus 2 cornerbacks, leaves 1 deep safety. Beat him and the run can go the distance.

quiz.q: On a run play, a lineman "climbs." What does that mean?
o: He leaves the line to block a linebacker
He jumps to block a kick
He pulls across to the other side
He moves before the snap (a false start)
quiz.w: After helping on a double-team at the line, one blocker lets go and moves up to block a linebacker at the second level (A in the diagram).

quiz.q: Ohio's Duncan Brune ran 91 yards for a TD on Tuesday. In the three-level picture, what had to happen?
o: Only the defensive line was blocked
He got past the linebackers, then past the last safety
The QB threw him a pass
Two deep safeties both missed him at the line
quiz.w: A long TD run means levels 1 and 2 were blocked (B) and the runner beat level 3, the safeties (C).
